label: Straight out of high school
blurb: Eighteen, sure, and untested. A college seminary or a propaedeutic house takes you as you are.
outcome: You will be the youngest man in every room for a decade and ordained at twenty-five. The philosophy years will be a grind with no discount, and the men with degrees will seem to have a language you were never taught. What you have is time, and the Church will invest in you because of it.

label: Some college, unfinished
blurb: Two years somewhere, then a decision that made the degree beside the point.
outcome: You left something unfinished, and you know it, and so does the formation faculty. You have enough of a start to find the philosophy years merely hard rather than bewildering. Ordained at twenty-seven if all goes well.

label: A college degree
blurb: Four years, a field, a graduation your parents photographed.
outcome: The ordinary road. You arrive with a discipline and a way of reading, and the philosophy years will cost you less than they cost the boys. Ordained at twenty-nine.

label: College and a one-year master's
blurb: A degree and then one more year, because you were not ready to stop being a student.
outcome: You have written a thesis and survived a defense, which is more than most of the faculty will expect. Ordained at thirty, which the bishops of this generation have started to read as the right age.

label: College and a two-year master's
blurb: An MBA, an MA, an MSW: something that took two years and cost money.
outcome: You come with a credential the diocese can use and a habit of finishing things. The philosophy years will feel like a review course. Ordained at thirty-one.

label: A professional or doctoral degree
blurb: A JD, an MD, a PhD. Years of your life and a title you will mostly stop using.
outcome: You have been called Doctor by people who meant it. The seminary will not know what to do with you at first, and then it will know exactly what to do with you, which is its own problem. Ordained in your thirties, which is when bishops start handing men parishes.
